title: Chronic Headache - Migraine History Taking
patient_instructions: You are Mary, a 30-year-old accountant. For 6 months you have had a headache that comes once or twice a week and is not getting better. You are worried and have had to take sick leave. If asked to describe it: it is always one-sided (sometimes left, sometimes right, but only one side per attack), throbbing/pulsatile, about 6-7/10, lasts several hours, and there is no radiation. It gets better if you lie in a dark, quiet room; nothing else helps. You feel very nauseated with the headache but have never vomited. You are sensitive to light and noise during attacks. You sometimes see sparkling/flashing lights before it starts (aura). Drinking wine can bring it on; certain foods do not. Your mother also had migraines. You take the combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP). You have NO: waking at night with pain, early-morning headache/vomiting, worsening with cough/sneeze, weakness, numbness, blurred vision, weight loss, fever, neck stiffness, head injury, or family history of cancer/brain tumour. You do not smoke, drink only occasional wine, take no other drugs, have no allergies. You live with your parents; no major stress at home or work. Ideas: you fear a brain tumour. Concerns: that something serious is being missed. Expectations: you want an explanation and a plan. Affect: anxious but cooperative; you relax when the doctor acknowledges your worry.
candidate_instructions: You are the GP. Mary, a 30-year-old woman, presents with a 6-month history of recurrent headache that is affecting her work and making her anxious. She is haemodynamically stable. Task: take a focused headache history, actively screen for red flags, reach a provisional diagnosis and briefly explain it to the patient with your reasoning and key differentials. You are NOT required to give a detailed management plan, but you should address contraception safety.
examiner_instructions: Look for a structured pain history (SIQORAA), elicitation of the migraine key features (nausea, photophobia/phonophobia, aura, wine trigger, family history) and deliberate screening of brain-tumour red flags (night waking, early-morning headache/vomiting, worse on cough/sneeze, focal neurology, weight loss, cancer history). A strong candidate applies ICHD-3 criteria to justify migraine and distinguishes migraine WITH aura from WITHOUT aura. The critical safety point: this patient has migraine WITH aura on a COCP - the candidate must recognise that oestrogen-containing contraception is contraindicated (stroke risk) and advise switching to a progestogen-only method. Do not accept the outdated 'blood vessels simply dilate' explanation as the sole model. Prompt only if stuck: 'Is there anything about her medications you are concerned about?'

criteria: Introduces self, addresses concern, confirms haemodynamic stability
Structured pain assessment (SIQORAA): site, intensity, quality, onset/timing, radiation, aggravating/relieving, effect on life
Elicits migraine key features: nausea, photophobia/phonophobia, aura, triggers (wine, food), family history
Screens contraception use and clarifies COCP vs progestogen-only
States provisional diagnosis of migraine with aura and justifies using ICHD-3 criteria
Actively screens and excludes brain-tumour red flags
Considers relevant differentials (tension, cluster, infection/meningitis, medication-overuse, trigeminal neuralgia)
Recognises migraine WITH aura + COCP as an absolute contraindication and advises stopping oestrogen-containing contraception
Provides red-flag safety-net and return advice
Empathic, patient-centred; explains diagnosis in accurate lay terms (neurovascular, not simply 'dilating blood vessels')
Checks understanding and responds to the patient's fear of a tumour

red_flags: Headache waking the patient at night, or early-morning headache with vomiting (raised intracranial pressure / tumour)
Headache worse on coughing, sneezing or straining
New focal neurological deficit - limb weakness, numbness/paraesthesiae, or blurred/loss of vision
Unexplained weight loss or a personal/family history of cancer including brain tumour
Fever with neck stiffness (meningitis) or thunderclap onset (subarachnoid haemorrhage)
australian_guidelines: eTG (Therapeutic Guidelines, Neurology): migraine is a primary neurovascular disorder; diagnose using ICHD-3 criteria and manage acute attacks with simple analgesia/NSAIDs +/- a triptan, documenting baseline blood pressure before prescribing a triptan.

eTG / Family Planning Australia (WHO MEC): migraine WITH aura is an absolute contraindication (MEC category 4) to any oestrogen-containing contraceptive at any age - switch to a progestogen-only option (POP, implant, or Mirena IUD).
RACGP / Murtagh safe diagnostic strategy: screen mandatory 'must-not-miss' red flags in every headache presentation even when the picture is a classic migraine.
learning_objectives: Take a structured headache history using SIQORAA and elicit the diagnostic features of migraine.
Apply ICHD-3 criteria and distinguish migraine with aura from migraine without aura.
Systematically screen for brain-tumour and other headache red flags.
Recognise the absolute contraindication to oestrogen-containing contraception in migraine with aura and counsel on safe alternatives.
Explain migraine to a patient in accurate, contemporary lay terms and provide a safety-net.
key_points: Unilateral throbbing headache relieved by rest in a dark quiet room, with nausea, photophobia and aura, is migraine until proven otherwise.
Aura (flashing/sparkling lights) plus COCP = absolute contraindication; stop the oestrogen-containing pill.
The vasodilation theory is outdated - explain migraine as a temporary change in how the nerves and blood vessels in the brain work.
Quantify analgesic-use days per month to screen for medication-overuse headache, and the menstrual relationship to screen for menstrual migraine.
A negative red-flag screen and fulfilment of ICHD-3 criteria justify the diagnosis without imaging.

citations.claim: The differential for a headache/facial-pain presentation includes migraine, cluster headache, trigeminal neuralgia, temporal arteritis and tumour.
Migraine is linked to combined oral contraception in the Australian reference literature, supporting the critical teaching point about stopping the COCP.
Screening the mandatory brain-tumour red flags even in a classic migraine reflects the safe diagnostic strategy of excluding serious disorders.
